cards.question: Explain why HI is less thermally stable than HCl. [2]
cards.answer: The larger iodine atom gives a longer H–I bond with poorer overlap [1]; its lower bond energy makes breaking it easier [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

cards.question: State which H–X bond value supports greater resistance to thermal bond breaking: a larger or smaller dissociation energy. [1]
cards.answer: A larger dissociation energy [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

cards.question: Determine the most thermally stable hydride from supplied bond energies HCl 431, HBr 366 and HI 299 kJ mol⁻¹. [1]
cards.answer: HCl [1], which has the largest bond energy.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

cards.question: Describe AgCl, AgBr and AgI in the aqueous silver-nitrate/ammonia comparison. [3]
cards.answer: AgCl is white and soluble in dilute ammonia [1]; AgBr is cream and partially soluble in dilute ammonia, dissolving more fully in concentrated ammonia [1]; AgI is yellow and insoluble in dilute ammonia [1].

cards.question: Write the precipitation half of the chloride test as an ionic equation, including state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s). Correct species/states [1]; atom/charge balance [1].

cards.question: Write the balanced redox equation for HBr reducing concentrated sulphuric acid to SO2, with Br2 and water as the other products. [2]
cards.answer: 2HBr + H2SO4 → Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O. Correct reactants/products [1]; balance [1].

cards.question: Explain why bromide reacting with concentrated sulphuric acid involves redox while the ordinary chloride/HCl displacement does not. [2]
cards.answer: Bromide is oxidised from −1 to 0 as Br2 forms [1], while sulphur is reduced from +6 to +4 in SO2; the chloride displacement has no corresponding oxidation-number changes [1].

cards.question: Describe chlorine disproportionation with cold dilute and hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide, using chlorine oxidation numbers. [3]
cards.answer: Cold dilute alkali gives chloride and chlorate(I) [1]; hot concentrated alkali gives chloride and chlorate(V) [1]; chlorine 0 is reduced to −1 and oxidised to +1 or +5 respectively [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The reactions of chlorine with aqueous sodium hydroxide

cards.question: Explain why Cl2 + 2OH− → Cl− + ClO− + H2O in cold dilute alkali is disproportionation. [2]
cards.answer: Chlorine 0 is reduced to −1 in Cl− [1] and oxidised to +1 in ClO− in the same overall reaction [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The reactions of chlorine with aqueous sodium hydroxide

cards.question: Describe the qualitative concentration response of Cl2 + H2O ⇌ H+ + Cl− + HOCl when acid is added, alkali removes H+, and pH rises in the HOCl/ClO− pair. [3]
cards.answer: Adding H+ favours chlorine on the left [1]; removing H+ favours the right-hand mixture [1]; higher pH favours ClO− relative to HOCl [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The reactions of chlorine with aqueous sodium hydroxide

cards.question: Write the balanced equation showing chlorine release from acidifying a chloride/chlorate(I) mixture, including aqueous states. [2]
cards.answer: ClO−(aq) + Cl−(aq) + 2H+(aq) → Cl2(g) + H2O(l). Correct species/states [1]; atom and charge balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The reactions of chlorine with aqueous sodium hydroxide

cards.question: Explain why raising pH favours ClO− in the qualitative HOCl ⇌ H+ + ClO− balance. [2]
cards.answer: Higher pH means lower H+ concentration [1]; the equilibrium response forms more H+ and ClO− from HOCl [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The reactions of chlorine with aqueous sodium hydroxide

cards.question: Describe the use of chlorine in water treatment through the active species, action and need for control. [3]
cards.answer: Water reaction forms oxidants including HOCl [1], which damage biological material and aid disinfection [1]; pH and oxidant concentration/contact need controlled monitoring [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some important uses of halogens and of halogen compounds

cards.question: Explain why water pH can affect chlorine-based disinfection. [2]
cards.answer: It changes the relative HOCl and ClO− amounts [1]; these species differ in disinfecting effectiveness, so oxidant identity as well as total amount matters [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some important uses of halogens and of halogen compounds

cards.question: State two industrial uses of halogen compounds besides water disinfection. [1]
cards.answer: For example, bleaching and PVC manufacture [1]; suitable solvent or refrigerant/propellant examples are also valid.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some important uses of halogens and of halogen compounds

cards.question: Suggest why a persistent chlorine-containing refrigerant can cause an environmental concern in the stratosphere. [1]
cards.answer: Its breakdown can release chlorine radicals that catalyse ozone destruction [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some important uses of halogens and of halogen compounds

cards.question: State the chemical process responsible for bleaching by chlorine-containing oxidants. [1]
cards.answer: Oxidation of colour-causing chemical species [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some important uses of halogens and of halogen compounds

cards.question: Explain why loss of colour in a bleach demonstration does not by itself establish complete water purification. [2]
cards.answer: It tests reaction with a colour-causing substance [1]; other biological or chemical quality criteria need their own assessment [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some important uses of halogens and of halogen compounds

cards.question: Identify the electron pair that allows NH3 to accept H+ and form NH4+. [1]
cards.answer: The lone pair on nitrogen [1].

cards.question: Draw NH4+ with its tetrahedral arrangement, showing four N–H bonds, the overall charge and whether nitrogen has a lone pair. [2]
cards.answer:
Four N–H bonds around N with no N lone pair [1]; tetrahedral representation with overall + charge, approximately 109.5° [1].

Central N has four N–H bonds, no lone pair and tetrahedral geometry. Two lines lie in the page, a solid wedge points towards the viewer and a hashed bond away. Brackets show total positive charge. Schematic projection, angles about 109.5 degrees.

cards.question: State two pathways by which farming can deplete soil nutrients. [1]
cards.answer: Removal in harvested material and loss through water-driven leaching [1].

cards.question: Explain why a field can lose nitrogen even when much of the crop remains locally. [2]
cards.answer: Dissolved nitrogen-containing species such as nitrate can be carried by moving water [1]; leaching can move them below roots or into drainage, removing available nutrient from the field [1].

cards.question: Describe why atmospheric nitrogen is difficult to use directly and why industrial ammonia manufacture is useful for fertilisers. [3]
cards.answer: N2 has a strong triple bond [1], giving a large barrier and low ordinary reactivity [1]; conversion to ammonia and salts supplies chemically accessible nitrogen compounds [1].

cards.question: Explain why plentiful N2 in air does not by itself provide readily reacting fertiliser nitrogen. [2]
cards.answer: Its strong N≡N bond makes ordinary chemical conversion difficult [1]; a specialised biological or industrial pathway is needed to produce suitable available compounds [1].

cards.question: Describe nitrogen’s oxidation numbers in NH3, N2, N2O and NO3−, and the direction from NH3 to nitrate. [3]
cards.answer: NH3 −3 and N2 0 [1]; N2O average +1 and NO3− +5 [1]; NH3 to nitrate raises the value and is oxidation [1].

cards.question: Explain why N2O has average nitrogen oxidation number +1 rather than +2 per nitrogen. [2]
cards.answer: Oxygen at −2 requires the two nitrogens together to contribute +2 [1]; dividing by two nitrogen atoms gives the average +1 [1].

cards.question: State an industrial use of ammonia relevant to crop nutrition. [1]
cards.answer: Manufacturing nitrogen fertilisers, including ammonium salts [1].

cards.question: Suggest how ammonia can be converted into ammonium sulphate. [1]
cards.answer: React it with sulphuric acid: 2NH3 + H2SO4 → (NH4)2SO4 [1].

cards.question: Describe three linked environmental consequences of highly soluble nitrate fertiliser being transported by water. [3]
cards.answer: Rapid leaching can remove nutrient from roots [1]; enrichment of surface waters can contribute to eutrophication and oxygen depletion [1]; groundwater or borehole sources can become nitrate-contaminated [1].

cards.question: Explain how nutrient enrichment can harm fish through eutrophication. [2]
cards.answer: It can stimulate excessive aquatic growth [1]; decomposition of dead material consumes dissolved oxygen, reducing what is available to fish [1].

cards.question: Describe a potential benefit, chemical reason and limitation of an organic fertiliser with less immediately soluble nutrient material. [3]
cards.answer: Lower immediate leaching can retain nutrient [1] because release into solution is slower [1]; release timing and soluble fractions vary, so pollution is not eliminated [1].

cards.question: Explain why lower immediate solubility can reduce early nutrient loss from a fertiliser. [2]
cards.answer: Less nutrient enters moving soil water at once [1], so a smaller amount can be carried away before later release and uptake [1].

cards.question: State two syllabus sources of atmospheric sulphur dioxide. [1]
cards.answer: Burning sulphur-containing fossil fuel and roasting sulphide ores [1].

cards.question: Suggest why burning two equal fuel masses can give different potential SO2 amounts. [1]
cards.answer: Their sulphur contents may differ [1], giving different sulphur amounts available for oxidation.

cards.question: State one breathing-related and one environmental consequence of SO2 pollution. [1]
cards.answer: Breathing difficulties/respiratory effects and contribution to acid rain [1].

cards.question: Suggest why sulphur dioxide pollution can damage limestone structures after atmospheric chemical changes. [1]
cards.answer: It contributes to acidic deposition, whose H+ reacts with the carbonate building material [1].

cards.question: State why using low-sulphur fuel is relevant to the syllabus’s vehicle and power-station example. [1]
cards.answer: It reduces the sulphur available to form SO2 and helps control pollutant exposure [1].

cards.question: Suggest what extra evidence is needed before claiming that a named station meets an applicable SO2 requirement. [1]
cards.answer: Relevant current measurements with the correct averaging/measurement basis and the actual applicable requirement [1]; a low-sulphur label alone is insufficient.

cards.question: Describe a functional group, a nucleophile and an electrophile. [3]
cards.answer: A functional group supplies characteristic chemical behaviour [1]; a nucleophile donates an electron pair [1]; an electrophile accepts an electron pair [1].

cards.question: Explain how the two propagation steps Cl• + CH4 → HCl + CH3• and CH3• + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl• sustain a radical chain, identifying the intermediate and electron feature. [2]
cards.answer: The first step makes the methyl-radical intermediate CH3• with an unpaired electron [1]; it forms the C–Cl product bond in the second step while a chlorine radical is regenerated, allowing another cycle [1]. These are single-electron changes, not a claim that the carbon radical has a negative charge.

cards.question: Draw electron-movement arrows for Cl–Cl homolysis and for C–Br heterolysis in which both bonding electrons go to bromine. Include the fragment charges or radical dots. [2]
cards.answer:
Homolysis: two fishhook arrows from the bond, one towards each Cl, giving 2Cl• [1]. Heterolysis: a full-headed curved arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, giving a positive carbon fragment and Br− [1].

Upper row shows homolysis of a Cl–Cl bond with two single-electron fishhook arrows, one to each Cl. Lower row shows heterolysis of C–Br with a full-headed pair arrow from the bond to Br, yielding a positive carbon fragment and bromide. Schematic fission, not a claim of reaction conditions.

cards.question: Name CH3CH(OH)CH3 systematically. [1]
cards.answer: Propan-2-ol [1].

cards.question: Suggest the systematic name for CH2ClCH2CH2CH3 using the lowest permitted halogen locant. [1]
cards.answer: 1-Chlorobutane [1].

cards.question: Identify the approximate angle at each carbon in ethene. [1]
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Shapes of organic molecules AND Infra-red spectroscopy

cards.question: Draw ethene with its carbon–carbon double bond, planar arrangement and approximate angle at carbon. [2]
cards.answer:
Show CH2=CH2 with the four C–H bonds and planar arrangement [1]; label approximately 120° at carbon [1].

Two carbon atoms joined by a double bond. Each carbon joins two hydrogens in one plane; angles approximately 120 degrees. Schematic lengths.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Shapes of organic molecules AND Infra-red spectroscopy

cards.question: Identify the local geometry at the carbonyl carbon of propanone. [1]
cards.answer: Approximately trigonal planar [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Shapes of organic molecules AND Infra-red spectroscopy

cards.question: Draw the local carbon arrangement of chloromethane, showing four bonds and an appropriate three-dimensional convention. Label the approximate bond angle. [2]
cards.answer: Carbon has three H and one Cl arranged tetrahedrally, with wedge/hashed depth where needed [1]; angles approximately 109.5° [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Shapes of organic molecules AND Infra-red spectroscopy

cards.question: State what molecular feature commonly produces a strong IR band in the supplied reference range 1670–1750 cm⁻¹. [1]
cards.answer: A carbonyl C=O group [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Shapes of organic molecules AND Infra-red spectroscopy

cards.question:
Determine the functional group supported by the labelled strong band in this synthetic IR spectrum. Supplied reference: strong C=O absorption 1670–1750 cm⁻¹. [1]

Original model percentage-transmittance spectrum with decreasing wavenumber from 4000 to 500 cm^-1, a sharp strong carbonyl-like band at 1720, plus illustrative C–H and fingerprint-region bands. It is not an experimental spectrum or unique compound identification.
cards.answer: A carbonyl C=O group [1], supported by the labelled 1720 cm⁻¹ absorption. This alone does not uniquely identify the molecule.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Shapes of organic molecules AND Infra-red spectroscopy

cards.question: Identify the general composition of an open-chain alkane with n carbon atoms.
cards.answer: CnH2n+2.

cards.question: Draw a displayed structure of ethane and a skeletal structure of butane.
cards.answer: Displayed ethane: two C joined by one bond, each C bearing three explicit H atoms and their bonds. Skeletal butane: a three-segment, four-position zigzag. See assets/8224-alkane-representations.png; no extra carbon is implied by a bond line.

cards.question: Name CH3C(CH3)2CH2CH2CH2CH3.
cards.answer: 2,2-dimethylhexane.

cards.question: Suggest the correct alkane name for CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3.
cards.answer: 2-methylbutane; the longest chain has four carbons and the branch receives locant 2.

cards.question: State how many hydrogens are attached to an alkane carbon bonded to three other carbons.
cards.answer: One hydrogen.

cards.question: Determine the molecular composition of CH3C(CH3)2CH2CH3.
cards.answer: C6H14: four CH3 groups, one CH2 and one carbon with no H.

cards.question: Describe three structural reasons for the general resistance of alkanes to polar attack.
cards.answer: Strong C–C/C–H bonds; little bond polarity; absence of a reactive electron-rich multiple bond or suitable electron-deficient carbon centre.

cards.question: Explain why ethane resists rapid bromine addition without radical-initiating light.
cards.answer: It lacks an electron-rich C=C pair for electrophilic addition, and its strong nearly non-polar single bonds do not supply that ionic addition pathway.

cards.question: Describe complete combustion and light-initiated halogen substitution of ethane.
cards.answer: Sufficient oxygen gives CO2 and water with energy release; suitable light enables chlorine or bromine to replace an H; the substitution produces a haloethane and a hydrogen halide.

cards.question: Write the balanced complete combustion equation for ethane, with hot gaseous products and state symbols.
Write the equation for one bromine substitution in ethane under radical-initiating light.
cards.answer: C2H6 + Br2 → C2H5Br + HBr; suitable radical-initiating light.

cards.question: Explain why prolonged ethane chlorination can give more than one substituted product.
cards.answer: The first chloroethane product retains C–H bonds, so further light-initiated radical substitution can replace more H atoms and produce a mixture.

cards.question: Describe initiation, propagation and combination termination in ethane chlorination.
cards.answer: Initiation forms radicals by light-induced Cl–Cl homolysis; propagation consumes a radical and makes another through hydrogen abstraction then halogen transfer; termination joins radicals without producing a radical.

cards.question: Explain how the ethane chlorination chain regenerates its reactive radical.
cards.answer: Cl• abstracts H: Cl• + C2H6 → HCl + C2H5•. The ethyl radical intermediate takes Cl from Cl2: C2H5• + Cl2 → C2H5Cl + Cl•. Single-electron movement forms the new bonds and regenerates Cl•.

cards.question: Draw the initiation of ethane chlorination, including single-electron arrows.
cards.answer: Draw Cl–Cl with two fishhook arrows from the bond, one to each Cl, with light over the reaction arrow, giving Cl• + Cl•. Each atom receives one original bond electron; dots show unpaired electrons.

cards.question: Describe crude oil as a source of aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons.
cards.answer: It is a mixture containing different hydrocarbon families; distillation separates boiling-range fractions; separation and further refinery reactions supply aliphatic and benzene-type aromatic feedstocks.

cards.question: Explain why one crude-oil fraction cannot be assumed to be a pure alkane.
cards.answer: A fraction groups molecules by boiling behaviour and can contain several structures, so collection of a fraction does not establish one composition or connectivity.

cards.question: Describe cracking and its useful products.
cards.answer: Larger hydrocarbons undergo bond rearrangement at high temperature, sometimes with a catalyst; smaller alkanes can serve as fuels; alkenes provide reactive chemical and polymer feedstocks.

cards.question: Explain why C10H22 → C6H14 + C4H8 can represent useful cracking when C4H8 is an alkene.
cards.answer: The atoms are conserved while each product has lower Mr; the smaller alkane is a fuel and the alkene is a reactive feedstock. This represents one possible split, not a unique product mixture.

cards.question: Identify the general composition of an open-chain hydrocarbon containing one C=C bond.
cards.answer: CnH2n; n is at least 2.

cards.question: Draw a displayed structure of propene.
cards.answer: Draw CH2=CH–CH3 with each C–H bond explicit: two H at the first carbon, one at the second and three at the third; show the double bond and complete four bond contributions per C.

cards.question: Name CH3CH=CHCH2CH3.
cards.answer: Pent-2-ene.

cards.question: Suggest the correct name for CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3.
cards.answer: 2-methylbut-1-ene.

cards.question: State how many hydrogen atoms an alkene carbon bears if it has a double bond and two carbon single bonds.
cards.answer: Zero; the carbon already has four bond contributions.

cards.question: Determine the molecular composition of CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3.
Describe three additions across ethene C=C using hydrogen, steam and bromine.
cards.answer: Hydrogen with heated Ni gives ethane; steam with phosphoric-acid catalyst at elevated temperature and pressure gives ethanol reversibly; Br2 in a suitable non-aqueous medium gives 1,2-dibromoethane.

cards.question: Write the organic equation for cold, dilute, acidified manganate(VII) oxidation of ethene to its diol, using [O].
cards.answer: CH2=CH2 + [O] + H2O → HOCH2CH2OH. Cold, dilute, acidified manganate(VII).

cards.question: Write the organic oxidation equation for propene cleavage by hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII), using [O].
cards.answer: CH3CH=CH2 + 5[O] → CH3COOH + CO2 + H2O. Hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII).

cards.question: Explain why ordinary ionic HBr addition to propene gives mainly 2-bromopropane.
cards.answer: Protonation favours the more stable secondary carbocation over the primary alternative; a bromide pair then bonds to its central positive carbon, giving mainly 2-bromopropane.

cards.question: State what happens to the bond electron pair in heterolytic fission.
cards.answer: Both electrons go to one of the fragments.

cards.question: Suggest the charge on bromine after heterolytic H–Br cleavage with the pair transferred to bromine.
cards.answer: Br−.

cards.question: Describe the stages of bromine addition to ethene in a suitable non-aqueous medium.
cards.answer: Ethene polarises Br2 and donates its π pair to nearer Br as Br–Br breaks to Br−; a bridged bromonium intermediate forms; bromide attack opens it to give 1,2-dibromoethane.

cards.question: Explain the electron-pair movements in ordinary ionic HBr addition to propene giving its major product.
cards.answer: The π pair forms a bond to H while H–Br transfers its pair to Br, giving CH3CH+CH3 and Br−. A bromide lone pair then forms C–Br at the positive centre, producing 2-bromopropane.

cards.question: Draw the full curved arrows and intermediate for ordinary ionic HBr addition to propene giving its major product.
cards.answer: Draw π bond→H and H–Br bond→Br, then CH3–CH+–CH3 and :Br−. Draw a bromide lone-pair arrow→positive carbon to form CH3CHBrCH3. Full arrowheads show pairs; see assets/8224-propene-hbr-mechanism.png.

cards.question: Describe how alkyl substitution affects the stability of comparable carbocations.
cards.answer: Alkyl groups donate electron density inductively towards the electron-deficient centre; more attached alkyl groups give greater stabilisation; tertiary > secondary > primary.

cards.question: Explain the role of the secondary carbocation in ordinary ionic HBr addition to propene.
cards.answer: π electrons bond to H at the terminal carbon, giving the secondary CH3CH+CH3 intermediate. Two alkyl groups stabilise it by inductive donation; bromide pair attack then produces the major 2-bromopropane product.

cards.question: Draw the secondary carbocation from propene protonation and indicate alkyl inductive donation.
cards.answer: Draw CH3–CH+–CH3, with a positive charge at the central carbon and inductive-direction labels from both methyl groups towards that centre. These labels indicate electron-density donation, not complete bond-pair transfer.

cards.question: State whether addition polymerisation of ethene eliminates water.
cards.answer: It does not eliminate water or another small molecule in the overall addition process.

cards.question: Suggest the polymer made by addition polymerisation of CH2=CHCl.
cards.answer: Poly(chloroethene), PVC, with repeat unit [–CH2–CHCl–]n.

cards.question: State what happens to C=C when an alkene forms its simple addition-polymer backbone.
cards.answer: It becomes C–C as new single bonds link monomer-derived units.

cards.question: Determine the addition-polymer repeat unit from CH2=CHCH3.
cards.answer: [–CH2–CH(CH3)–]n, with chain-continuation bonds through the brackets.

cards.question: Explain why [–CH2=CH2–]n is an incorrect repeat unit for poly(ethene).
cards.answer: It retains C=C while adding external chain bonds, giving each carbon five bond contributions. Replace C=C by C–C to obtain [–CH2–CH2–]n; two C–H plus two C–C single bonds complete four per carbon.

cards.question: State the monomer corresponding to [–CH2–CHCl–]n.
cards.answer: CH2=CHCl, chloroethene.

cards.question: Suggest the monomer for the repeated chain pattern –CH2–CH(CH3)–.
cards.answer: CH2=CHCH3, propene.

cards.question: State the structural reason poly(ethene) is difficult to dispose of by ordinary biodegradation.
cards.answer: Its strong C–C backbone resists the usual biological breakdown processes.

cards.question: Suggest why a plastic film breaking into visible fragments does not demonstrate complete biodegradation.
cards.answer: Its polymer chains may remain in smaller plastic pieces; fragmentation alone does not show biological chemical conversion.

cards.question: State one practical obstacle to recycling mixed polymer waste.
cards.answer: Different polymer types or contamination can make sorting and reprocessing difficult.

cards.question: Suggest a supported waste route for clean, separately collected poly(ethene) offcuts accepted by a local recycler.
cards.answer: Mechanical recycling into another product; the stated clean, sorted material is accepted by the available facility.

cards.question: State the difference between water solubility and biodegradability of a polymer.
cards.answer: Solubility is dissolution in water; biodegradability is biological chemical breakdown under suitable settings.

cards.question: Suggest what can be concluded if a film dissolves in water but its recovered chains are unchanged.
cards.answer: The film is water-soluble; this observation does not demonstrate biodegradation.

cards.question: Describe why alkane combustion is useful in a stove, furnace and engine.
cards.answer: Its overall energy release can heat cookware, heat an industrial process and supply energy for mechanical work; bond formation in products releases more energy than reactant bond breaking requires.
